title: Module 6: Intellectual Property and Software Licensing · model visual
question: What protects the things you build with, and how do the four forms of intellectual property differ?
documentTitle: Module 6: Intellectual Property and Software Licensing

example.title: Illustrative case: a small team's app
example.description: A hypothetical app uses a library, an image, a font and a copied snippet. Each beat asks what protection or licence might apply to a component. This is not a legal verdict on any real use.

chapters.title: Everything you build borrows
chapters.question: What outside material does a typical project contain?

sources.title: Module 6: Intellectual Property and Software Licensing

chapters.narration: Almost nothing in a shipped app is truly original: libraries, artwork, fonts and pasted snippets all arrive with someone else's terms attached. Name each one, write down its licence or mark it unknown, and you have an inventory you can act on.

continuity.bridge: The same case, a different teaching move.

nodes.title: The product we ship
nodes.body: Take one imaginary app built by a team. It is the hub of the picture: every item around it is something the app leans on but did not make itself.

nodes.title: Third-party library
nodes.body: Reusable code someone else wrote and the app calls into. Hunt down its licence and record the terms; if they cannot be pinned down, mark it as unknown rather than guessing.

nodes.title: Picture or icon
nodes.body: A visual made by a different creator. Pictures count as creative output, so the conditions of use need checking before the artwork goes anywhere near the product.

nodes.title: Typeface file
nodes.body: The font files that render the app's words on screen. Each comes with its own conditions, so note those terms down or label the entry unknown.

nodes.title: Pasted code snippet
nodes.body: A block lifted from a discussion board or generated by an AI tool. Where it came from and what rules apply may be murky, and the honest entry reflects that gap.

nodes.title: Inventory of parts
nodes.body: One table listing each outside component alongside its licence, using unknown as a placeholder. Tally the unknowns, then hold the table for the later activity.

visual.takeaway: Almost nothing in a shipped app is truly original: libraries, artwork, fonts and pasted snippets all arrive with someone else's terms attached. Name each one, write down its licence or mark it unknown, and you have an inventory you can act on.

chapters.title: Four forms of protection under RA 8293
chapters.question: What does each form protect, how does it arise, and how long does it last?

sources.title: Module 6: Intellectual Property and Software Licensing

chapters.narration: Each right begins differently and lasts differently: copyright is automatic, patent depends on a grant, trade secrecy depends on confidentiality, and trademark continues through renewal.

continuity.bridge: The same case, a different teaching move.

nodes.title: Copyright
nodes.body: Once original code or a creative work is fixed in a tangible form, the law protects that particular expression while leaving the underlying idea free for others to use.
cells: The fixed expression of a work, not the idea itself
Arises automatically when the work is created and fixed
Generally the author's life plus 50 years

nodes.title: Patent
nodes.body: A new process or product can be protected only after examination confirms it is novel, inventive, and industrially useful; the right is granted rather than automatic.
cells: Inventions that satisfy the statutory tests
Requires an application and a successful grant
20 years counted from the filing date

nodes.title: Trade secret
nodes.body: Valuable non-public information stays protected only while the holder keeps it confidential; public disclosure normally ends the right.
cells: Confidential technical or business information with commercial value
Arises through secrecy and reasonable safeguards
Lasts indefinitely unless secrecy is lost

nodes.title: Trademark
nodes.body: A sign used in commerce identifies the source of goods or services; registration together with actual use builds exclusive rights in the mark.
cells: Distinctive marks that identify goods or services
Secured through registration and continued use
Can be renewed without a fixed end date

visual.takeaway: Each right begins differently and lasts differently: copyright is automatic, patent depends on a grant, trade secrecy depends on confidentiality, and trademark continues through renewal.

chapters.title: Fair use is weighed, not assumed
chapters.question: What is weighed for fair use, and what do people wrongly assume?

sources.title: Module 6: Intellectual Property and Software Licensing

chapters.narration: Fair use is a conclusion reached by weighing purpose, nature, amount, and market effect together; attribution and educational intent do not replace that analysis.

continuity.bridge: The same case, a different teaching move.

nodes.title: A copied function
nodes.body: Picture an app that lifts a short routine from a public code repository. Fair use is not a label you can attach up front; it emerges only after the four factors are weighed against one another.

nodes.title: Purpose and character
nodes.body: Examine why the material was used and whether the use transforms it. A teaching aim can tilt the balance, but a good motive does not settle the outcome on its own.

nodes.title: Nature of the source
nodes.body: Ask whether the copied work is factual or creative, published or unpublished. This factor joins the others in the balance and is never a standalone verdict.

nodes.title: Portion taken
nodes.body: Compare the size and significance of the excerpt with the source as a whole. Even a small share can matter, and this factor cannot resolve the case by itself.

nodes.title: Effect on the market
nodes.body: Trace whether the copying displaces sales, licensing, or demand for the original. That harm is assessed alongside purpose, nature, and amount, not in isolation.

nodes.title: Assumptions to drop
nodes.body: Crediting the creator does not supply a license, and a classroom setting is not an automatic shield. Attribution and education are considerations, not blanket permissions.

visual.takeaway: Fair use is a conclusion reached by weighing purpose, nature, amount, and market effect together; attribution and educational intent do not replace that analysis.

chapters.title: Read the conditions, not the label
chapters.question: What does each licence family permit, require and mean for a product?

sources.title: Module 6: Intellectual Property and Software Licensing

chapters.narration: Start with the grant and the trigger: permissive terms need notice, copyleft terms follow distribution, contracts define commercial limits, and silence grants nothing.

continuity.bridge: The same case, a different teaching move.

nodes.title: Public domain
nodes.body: The rights holder waives exclusive rights, so reusers owe no attribution or share-alike duty.
cells: Any purpose, including commercial use
No conditions attached
No compliance work needed

nodes.title: Permissive (MIT, BSD)
nodes.body: A broad grant allows reuse and adaptation, provided the copyright and licence notice travel with copies.
cells: Commercial use, modification and redistribution
Keep copyright and licence notice with copies
Low friction for closed products

nodes.title: Weak copyleft (LGPL)
nodes.body: Reciprocal rules attach to the library itself, so a larger product may combine it while changes to that library stay open.
cells: Combine with proprietary code through defined linking
Publish changes made to the covered component
Review linking method and share library edits

nodes.title: Strong copyleft (GPL)
nodes.body: Distributing the combined program triggers reciprocal terms, so the whole distributed work must use the same licence.
cells: Run and modify freely; distribute under the same terms
Provide source for the whole distributed work
Plan to open-source or avoid distribution

nodes.title: Proprietary or commercial
nodes.body: Rights come only from the contract; anything not expressly granted stays with the vendor.
cells: Only what the agreement expressly allows
Fees and limits on seats, copies or fields of use
Track usage to stay inside audit rights

nodes.title: No licence stated
nodes.body: Default copyright reserves all rights, so possession of the code does not imply permission to use it.
cells: No rights unless separately granted
Permission must be obtained from the owner
Do not ship or rely on it

visual.takeaway: Start with the grant and the trigger: permissive terms need notice, copyleft terms follow distribution, contracts define commercial limits, and silence grants nothing.

chapters.title: Walk the licence route
chapters.question: In order, what does each licence family permit and require, from least to most constraining?

sources.title: Module 6: Intellectual Property and Software Licensing

chapters.narration: Licence families form a scale of obligation: public domain asks nothing, permissive licences ask for credit, weak copyleft asks for component changes, strong copyleft extends sharing to the whole distributed work, proprietary licences limit use to a contract, and no licence grants no rights.

continuity.bridge: The same case, a different teaching move.

nodes.title: Open access
nodes.body: A public domain dedication removes copyright restrictions entirely: anyone may copy, change and redistribute the work without asking permission or carrying an obligation. For the app's library, the licence itself would impose no duty.

nodes.title: Keep the credit
nodes.body: Permissive licences such as MIT and BSD allow reuse, alteration and redistribution, including in paid products. The mechanism is attribution: the copyright notice and licence text must travel with the code.

nodes.title: Share the edits
nodes.body: Weak copyleft, as in LGPL, lets the component sit inside a larger proprietary application. The reciprocal duty is narrow: anyone who modifies the component itself must make those changes available, while ordinary linking remains allowed.

nodes.title: Whole-work share
nodes.body: Strong copyleft, such as GPL, permits use and modification, but distribution triggers a broader condition. The entire distributed work must carry the same licence, so releasing the app can require releasing its source.

nodes.title: Contract-only use
nodes.body: A proprietary or commercial licence grants only the rights written into the agreement. Payment, seat counts and usage caps define the boundary; going past those limits can expose the organisation to an audit or breach claim.

nodes.title: Silence means no
nodes.body: If a project carries no licence at all, copyright law grants no permission by default. Being publicly visible is not the same as being reusable, so copying or shipping the code without authorisation is not free use.

visual.takeaway: Licence families form a scale of obligation: public domain asks nothing, permissive licences ask for credit, weak copyleft asks for component changes, strong copyleft extends sharing to the whole distributed work, proprietary licences limit use to a contract, and no licence grants no rights.

chapters.title: Open source runs on reciprocity
chapters.question: What three obligations come with taking part in open source?

roles.permission: Confirm you are allowed to contribute
roles.licences: Follow the licences already in the code
roles.fairness: Do not take without giving back
roles.commons: Remember the shared pool you draw from

sources.title: Module 6: Intellectual Property and Software Licensing

chapters.narration: Contributing openly carries three duties: check you have the right to share, respect every licence bundled into the code, and return value to the commons instead of only consuming it.

continuity.bridge: The same case, a different teaching move.

nodes.title: Confirm you are allowed to contribute
nodes.body: Before you publish any code you wrote on the job, read your employment contract. It decides whether your employer owns that work and whether you can share it at all.

nodes.title: Follow the licences already in the code
nodes.body: Each borrowed library arrives with its own terms. Keep the notices intact and, when a licence demands it, publish the source. The specific licence tells you which duty applies.

nodes.title: Do not take without giving back
nodes.body: Using someone else's work while ignoring its conditions erodes the shared pool everyone relies on. Treat this as a community norm rather than a legal rule.

nodes.title: Remember the shared pool you draw from
nodes.body: The borrowed component lives in a common repository, and your team's app is built on top of it. Every obligation above ties your project back to that shared resource.

visual.takeaway: Contributing openly carries three duties: check you have the right to share, respect every licence bundled into the code, and return value to the commons instead of only consuming it.

chapters.title: Who owns what you write at work
chapters.question: How do the IP Code and your employment agreement together decide ownership?

sources.title: Module 6: Intellectual Property and Software Licensing

chapters.narration: The statute sets the default, but your contract can shift it: read the assignment clause, check whether it covers only work duties or your whole employment, and secure a written carve-out for anything you want to keep.

continuity.bridge: The same case, a different teaching move.

nodes.title: Read the assignment clause
nodes.body: Before you sign, locate the wording that hands ownership of your creations to the employer. A broad assignment can reach far beyond office tasks — side projects, thesis code and open source patches may all be swept in, so identify exactly what the text claims.

nodes.title: Measure how far it reaches
nodes.body: Two versions look alike but behave very differently: one covers only work produced in the course of your duties, the other covers anything you make while employed. A weekend app built for fun sits outside the narrow version and inside the wide one, so read the boundary words carefully.

nodes.title: Negotiate a written carve-out
nodes.body: A carve-out is an explicit exception naming the work the clause will not touch. If a personal project matters to you, get that exclusion recorded on paper before signing rather than trusting that nobody will enforce the default rule later.

nodes.title: Keep personal work separate
nodes.body: Build your own things on your own hours and your own hardware, and avoid mixing them with company repositories or accounts. That separation strengthens your position, yet it does not override the contract — the clause's wording still settles who owns the result.

visual.takeaway: The statute sets the default, but your contract can shift it: read the assignment clause, check whether it covers only work duties or your whole employment, and secure a written carve-out for anything you want to keep.

chapters.title: Apply it: audit and assess
chapters.question: How do you audit a project and approach the assessment items?

sources.title: Module 6: Intellectual Property and Software Licensing

chapters.narration: An audit is only as strong as its record: name every component, read the actual licence terms, and separate credit from permission. Where evidence or classification is missing, label the gap instead of guessing.

continuity.bridge: The same case, a different teaching move.

nodes.title: The project as audit record
nodes.body: Begin with the project itself. For each component, capture the licence it carries, the duty that licence creates, and whether your current use satisfies that duty.

nodes.title: Library licence
nodes.body: List the exact licence for the library rather than assuming one rule covers every package. Different licence families impose different conditions, so read the actual terms and note whether you have met each condition.

nodes.title: Image rights
nodes.body: Trace the image to its source and record the licence attached to it. A credit line only identifies the creator; it does not grant reuse rights, so unresolved or missing permission must be treated as a problem.

nodes.title: Copied code with no licence
nodes.body: Code taken from a repository that displays no licence comes with no stated permission. Mark its status as unresolved, then gather more information or replace it before calling the audit complete.

nodes.title: AI-assisted code
nodes.body: Describe how you handled code produced with an AI assistant and keep that decision in the audit trail. The supplied material leaves the classification open, so the important move is to document your chosen treatment.

nodes.title: Missing assessment inputs
nodes.body: Some assessment inputs are absent: Case 5 in Appendix C.2, the answer keys, and rubrics R-1 through R-3. Without them, Activity 6.2 and the grading questions cannot be completed from this material alone.

visual.takeaway: An audit is only as strong as its record: name every component, read the actual licence terms, and separate credit from permission. Where evidence or classification is missing, label the gap instead of guessing.
